questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Apply the condition for conduction and displacement currents to be comparable
questions.stem: In a study group revision, when are conduction and displacement currents comparable in a material

options.text: When sigma over omega epsilon is of order one
When the material is a perfect conductor

questions.explanation: The ratio of conduction to displacement current is sigma over omega epsilon. When this is of order one, the two currents are comparable. At extremes one dominates.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wire's resistance rises at radio frequency
questions.stem: Explain why a wire's resistance rises at radio frequency in a revision note

answer.exemplar: At radio frequency the skin effect reduces the effective conducting area, so the same current passes through a smaller region, raising the resistance above its DC value.

questions.explanation: The skin effect confines current to a surface layer. Reduced effective area means higher resistance for the same material and length.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain the origin of cutoff frequency in a waveguide
questions.stem: Why does a waveguide have a cutoff frequency

options.text: Because the guide walls are too thin
Because the transverse wavelength must fit across the guide
Because the guide is too long
Because the source is too weak

questions.explanation: Cutoff arises because the wave must fit transversely across the guide; below cutoff the required transverse wavenumber becomes imaginary and propagation ceases. Wall thickness and length are not the cause.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Compute the cutoff frequency of a rectangular waveguide
questions.stem: A rectangular guide has width a = 2 cm; find the cutoff frequency of the TE10 mode in MHz using c = 3e8 m/s
questions.explanation: Cutoff frequency f_c equals c over 2a for TE10. With a = 0.02 m, f_c is 3e8 divided by 0.04, which is 7.5e9 Hz, i.e. 7500 MHz. Using a instead of 2a gives 15000 MHz.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Determine the cutoff wavelength of the next higher mode
questions.stem: For a rectangular guide of width a, what is the cutoff wavelength of the TE20 mode
questions.explanation: TE_m0 cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so TE20 gives 2a over 2, which is a. TE10 gives 2a. The next mode has half the cutoff wavelength.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Describe waveguide behaviour below cutoff
questions.stem: What happens to a signal sent below a waveguide's cutoff frequency

options.text: It converts to a TEM mode

questions.explanation: Below cutoff the propagation constant becomes imaginary, so the field decays exponentially along the guide rather than propagating. No real propagation occurs.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Compute the guide wavelength at a given operating frequency
questions.stem: A guide has cutoff 6 GHz and is fed at 10 GHz; find the guide wavelength in cm if free-space wavelength is 3 cm
questions.explanation: Guide wavelength lambda_g equals lambda_0 divided by sqrt(1 minus (f_c over f)^2). With f_c/f = 0.6, sqrt(1-0.36)=0.8, so lambda_g = 3/0.8 = 3.75 cm. Using multiplication gives 2.4 cm.

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Explain why TE10 is the dominant mode in a rectangular guide
questions.stem: Explain why the TE10 mode is called the dominant mode in a rectangular waveguide

answer.exemplar: TE10 has the lowest cutoff frequency among all modes, so it is the first to propagate as frequency rises and dominates the guide's usable band.

questions.explanation: Dominant means lowest cutoff. TE10's cutoff is c over 2a, lower than any other TE or TM mode, so it propagates first.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about comparability of the two currents
questions.stem: Stage one: what is the ratio of conduction to displacement current; stage two: when are they comparable

options.text: omega epsilon over sigma; when it is large
sigma over omega epsilon; when it is of order one
sigma times omega epsilon; when it is zero
sigma plus omega epsilon; when it is infinite

questions.explanation: The ratio is sigma over omega epsilon. Comparability occurs when this ratio is of order one, neither very large nor very small.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a claim about RF wire resistance
questions.stem: A note claims a wire's resistance is the same at radio frequency as at DC; find the error

options.text: Skin effect raises resistance at RF
Resistance drops to zero at RF

questions.explanation: At RF the skin effect reduces effective area, raising resistance above the DC value. The DC resistance is a lower bound only.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of cutoff frequencies and identify the dominant mode

stimulus.body: Cutoff table for a = 2 cm guide: TE10 7.5 GHz; TE20 15 GHz; TE01 15 GHz; TE11 16.8 GHz. License original.

questions.stem: Which mode is dominant according to the table
questions.explanation: TE10 has the lowest cutoff frequency, 7.5 GHz, so it is the dominant mode. The other modes cut in at higher frequencies.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute cutoff frequency from a table of widths
questions.stem: A guide has width 3 cm; find the TE10 cutoff frequency in GHz using c = 3e8 m/s
questions.explanation: f_c equals c over 2a, which is 3e8 divided by 0.06, equal to 5e9 Hz, i.e. 5 GHz. Using a instead of 2a gives 10 GHz.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a cutoff wavelength claim
questions.stem: A note claims TE20 has the same cutoff wavelength as TE10; find the error

options.text: TE20 cutoff wavelength is half that of TE10
TE20 cutoff wavelength is double that of TE10

questions.explanation: TE_m0 cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so TE20's cutoff wavelength a is half of TE10's 2a. The claim ignores the mode index.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about below-cutoff behaviour
questions.stem: Below cutoff, a waveguide behaves like
questions.explanation: A waveguide passes frequencies above cutoff and attenuates those below, so it acts as a high-pass filter. Below cutoff the field is evanescent.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a guide-wavelength computation
questions.stem: A computation multiplies free-space wavelength by sqrt(1-(f_c/f)^2) instead of dividing; find the error

options.text: Guide wavelength requires division, not multiplication
The square root should be squared

questions.explanation: Guide wavelength equals free-space wavelength divided by sqrt(1-(f_c/f)^2). Multiplication inverts the relation and gives too small a value.

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about dominant mode and cutoff
questions.stem: Stage one: which mode has the lowest cutoff; stage two: why is it called dominant

options.text: TE20; because it has highest power
TE10; because it propagates first as frequency rises

questions.explanation: TE10 has the lowest cutoff frequency, so it is the first mode to propagate when frequency increases from zero, hence dominant.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Numerically evaluate the ratio sigma over omega epsilon
questions.stem: Given sigma = 1 S/m, epsilon = 8.85e-12 F/m, f = 1e9 Hz, find the ratio sigma over omega epsilon
questions.explanation: omega is 2 pi f, about 6.28e9. omega epsilon is about 5.56e-2. sigma over that is 1 over 5.56e-2, about 18.0. Using sigma = 1e-3 gives 0.018.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about RF resistance and skin depth
questions.stem: Stage one: what happens to skin depth as frequency rises; stage two: what happens to wire resistance
questions.explanation: Rising frequency shrinks skin depth, reducing effective area and raising resistance. The two trends move together.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about cutoff and guide width
questions.stem: How does widening a waveguide affect its cutoff frequency
questions.explanation: Cutoff frequency is inversely proportional to guide width, so widening lowers the cutoff. The first mode to propagate shifts down in frequency.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Diagram interpretation of cutoff frequency versus width
questions.stem: A diagram plots cutoff frequency versus guide width as a hyperbola; the curve indicates

options.misconception: would be a straight line through origin

questions.explanation: Cutoff frequency is inversely proportional to width, giving a hyperbola on the plot. Direct proportionality would be a rising straight line.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the cutoff wavelength for TE30
questions.stem: For a guide of width a = 4 cm, find the TE30 cutoff wavelength in cm
questions.explanation: TE_m0 cutoff wavelength is 2a over m. For TE30 with a = 4 cm, that is 8 over 3, about 2.67 cm. Using 2a over 2 gives 4 cm, the TE20 value.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Explain evanescent decay below cutoff
questions.stem: Explain what happens to a signal below a waveguide's cutoff frequency

answer.exemplar: Below cutoff the propagation constant becomes imaginary, so the field decays exponentially along the guide instead of propagating, and no power is transmitted.

questions.explanation: The imaginary propagation constant produces evanescent decay. Energy is reflected rather than transmitted along the guide.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a guide-wavelength value
questions.stem: A table lists guide wavelength 2.4 cm for a guide with f_c/f = 0.6 and free-space wavelength 3 cm; find the error
questions.explanation: Guide wavelength is 3 divided by 0.8, which is 3.75 cm. The listed 2.4 cm comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of cutoff frequencies and identify dominant mode

stimulus.body: Cutoff table: TE10 7.5 GHz; TE20 15 GHz; TE01 15 GHz; TM11 16.8 GHz. License original.

questions.stem: Which mode dominates the usable band
questions.explanation: TE10 has the lowest cutoff at 7.5 GHz, so it dominates the usable band from 7.5 GHz upward until TE20 cuts in at 15 GHz.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about good versus poor conductor
questions.stem: In a good conductor at low frequency, which current dominates
questions.explanation: In a good conductor sigma over omega epsilon is very large, so conduction current dominates. Displacement current matters more in insulators.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute AC resistance ratio from skin depth
questions.stem: A wire has radius 2 mm and skin depth 0.2 mm; estimate the ratio of AC to DC resistance
questions.explanation: AC resistance is inversely proportional to effective area, so R_ac over R_dc equals (pi r^2) over (2 pi r delta), which is r over (2 delta), equal to 2 over 0.4, which is 5.0. Using 2 delta over r gives 0.2.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about cutoff and operating frequency
questions.stem: Stage one: what must operating frequency be relative to cutoff; stage two: what happens if it is below

options.text: Above cutoff; propagates; below cutoff, evanescent decay

questions.explanation: Propagation requires operating frequency above cutoff. Below cutoff the field decays exponentially and no power is transmitted.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a cutoff frequency computation
questions.stem: A computation uses c over a instead of c over 2a for TE10 cutoff; find the error

options.text: The denominator should be 2a, not a

questions.explanation: TE10 cutoff is c over 2a. Using c over a doubles the frequency. The factor of 2 comes from the half-wavelength fit across the width.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about mode spacing
questions.stem: As mode index m increases in TE_m0, what happens to cutoff wavelength
questions.explanation: Cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so it decreases as m increases. Higher modes have shorter cutoff wavelengths and higher cutoff frequencies.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about below-cutoff field
questions.stem: Stage one: is the propagation constant real or imaginary below cutoff; stage two: what is the field behaviour
questions.explanation: Below cutoff the propagation constant is imaginary, producing exponential decay of the field along the guide. The field is nonzero but evanescent.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute guide wavelength
questions.stem: A guide has f_c = 5 GHz and is fed at 10 GHz; free-space wavelength is 3 cm. Find guide wavelength in cm

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Explain dominance in terms of usable bandwidth
questions.stem: Explain why the dominant mode is preferred in waveguide design

answer.exemplar: The dominant mode has the lowest cutoff, giving the widest single-mode operating band before the next mode cuts in, simplifying design and avoiding mode competition.

questions.explanation: Using the dominant mode maximises the frequency range with only one propagating mode, preventing intermodal interference.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of material regimes and identify comparability

stimulus.body: Regime table: copper at 1 MHz ratio 1e8; seawater at 1 MHz ratio 4; glass at 1 MHz ratio 1e-4. License original.

questions.stem: Which material in the table has comparable conduction and displacement currents
questions.explanation: Seawater has ratio of order one, so its conduction and displacement currents are comparable. Copper and glass are at opposite extremes.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about conductor geometry at RF
questions.stem: To reduce RF resistance, a designer should

options.text: Use a single thick solid conductor
options.misconception: thick core is unused at RF

options.text: Use a hollow tube or Litz wire

questions.explanation: A hollow tube puts material where current actually flows, and Litz wire reduces skin-effect losses. A thick solid conductor wastes interior material.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a cutoff explanation
questions.stem: A note attributes cutoff to the guide being too short; find the error

options.text: Cutoff depends on transverse width, not length

questions.explanation: Cutoff is a transverse resonance condition depending on guide width. Length affects matching and resonances but not the cutoff frequency itself.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about cutoff and width change
questions.stem: Stage one: if width doubles, what happens to cutoff; stage two: what happens to the dominant mode's band

options.text: Cutoff halves; band shifts down and widens

questions.explanation: Doubling width halves cutoff frequency, shifting the operating band downward. The relative bandwidth may change depending on the next mode.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Diagram interpretation of mode cutoff wavelengths
questions.stem: A diagram shows bars of decreasing height for TE10, TE20, TE30 cutoff wavelengths; the trend indicates

options.text: Cutoff wavelength increases with mode index
Cutoff wavelength decreases with mode index

questions.explanation: Cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so it decreases as mode index rises. The bars of decreasing height reflect this.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the attenuation constant below cutoff
questions.stem: Below cutoff with f_c = 10 GHz and f = 6 GHz, find sqrt((f_c/f)^2 - 1)
questions.explanation: sqrt((10/6)^2 - 1) = sqrt(2.778 - 1) = sqrt(1.778) = 1.333. This factor governs the evanescent decay rate.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about guide wavelength versus free-space
questions.stem: How does guide wavelength compare to free-space wavelength above cutoff
questions.explanation: Guide wavelength equals free-space wavelength divided by sqrt(1-(f_c/f)^2), which is less than one, so the guide wavelength is longer. At cutoff it becomes infinite.
questions.hint: Division by a number less than one

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a claim about dominant mode
questions.stem: A note claims the dominant mode has the highest cutoff frequency; find the error

options.text: The dominant mode has the lowest cutoff

questions.explanation: Dominant refers to the mode with the lowest cutoff frequency, which propagates first. Highest cutoff would be the last mode to appear.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Explain the physical meaning of the ratio sigma over omega epsilon
questions.stem: Explain what the ratio sigma over omega epsilon tells us about a material

answer.exemplar: It compares conduction current density to displacement current density; a large value means conduction dominates, a small value means displacement dominates, and a value near one means they are comparable.

questions.explanation: The ratio directly compares the two current densities. It separates good conductors, lossy dielectrics, and good insulators by order of magnitude.
questions.hint: Ratio of the two current densities

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of AC resistance versus frequency and identify the trend

stimulus.body: AC resistance table for a fixed wire: 1 kHz 1.0 ohm; 1 MHz 3.2 ohm; 1 GHz 100 ohm. License original.

questions.stem: What does the table imply about skin effect
questions.explanation: Rising AC resistance with frequency reflects strengthening skin effect, which shrinks effective area. The trend is monotonic and steep at high frequency.
questions.hint: Rising resistance means stronger skin effect

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about cutoff and frequency band
questions.stem: A waveguide's single-mode band lies

options.misconception: below cutoff there is no propagation

questions.explanation: Single-mode operation occurs between the dominant mode's cutoff and the next higher mode's cutoff. Below dominant cutoff nothing propagates; above the next cutoff, multiple modes propagate.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of guide widths and find cutoff

stimulus.body: Width table: a = 1 cm cutoff 15 GHz; a = 2 cm cutoff 7.5 GHz; a = 3 cm cutoff 5 GHz. License original.

questions.stem: Which width gives the lowest cutoff frequency
questions.explanation: Wider guides have lower cutoff frequencies. The 3 cm guide has the lowest cutoff at 5 GHz.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about mode index and cutoff wavelength
questions.stem: Stage one: how does cutoff wavelength scale with mode index m; stage two: what is TE30's cutoff wavelength relative to TE10's
questions.explanation: Cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so it is inversely proportional to m. TE30's cutoff wavelength is one third of TE10's.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about below-cutoff power transmission
questions.stem: Below cutoff, how much power does a waveguide transmit
questions.explanation: Below cutoff the field is evanescent and carries no real power along the guide. Input power is reflected, not transmitted.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a guide-wavelength claim
questions.stem: A note claims guide wavelength is always shorter than free-space wavelength; find the error

options.text: Guide wavelength is longer above cutoff

questions.explanation: Guide wavelength equals free-space wavelength divided by sqrt(1-(f_c/f)^2), which is greater than one above cutoff, so it is longer. It is infinite only at cutoff.

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the dominant mode cutoff for a given width
questions.stem: For a guide of width 5 cm, find the dominant TE10 cutoff frequency in GHz using c = 3e8 m/s
questions.explanation: f_c = c over 2a = 3e8 over 0.1 = 3e9 Hz = 3 GHz. Using a instead of 2a gives 6 GHz.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about material regime and current dominance
questions.stem: Stage one: what does a very large sigma over omega epsilon imply; stage two: which current dominates

options.text: Displacement dominates; large ratio means displacement
Conduction dominates; large ratio means conduction
They are equal; large ratio means comparable
Neither flows; large ratio means insulator

questions.explanation: A large ratio means conduction current greatly exceeds displacement current. The material behaves as a conductor.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain why DC resistance is a lower bound for AC resistance
questions.stem: Explain why a wire's DC resistance is a lower bound for its AC resistance

answer.exemplar: DC uses the full cross-section, while AC at radio frequency uses only the skin-depth layer, so effective area shrinks and resistance rises above the DC value.

questions.explanation: The skin effect reduces usable area at AC. Since resistance is inversely proportional to area, AC resistance exceeds DC resistance.
questions.hint: AC area is smaller than DC area

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the dominant cutoff for a given width
questions.stem: Find the TE10 cutoff frequency in GHz for a guide of width 6 cm using c = 3e8 m/s
questions.explanation: f_c = 3e8 over 0.12 = 2.5e9 Hz = 2.5 GHz. Using a instead of 2a gives 5 GHz.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about cutoff and mode index
questions.stem: For fixed width, how does cutoff frequency change as mode index m increases
questions.explanation: Cutoff frequency is proportional to m over 2a, so it increases with mode index. Higher modes need higher frequencies to propagate.

questions.topic: Cutoff wavelength and the next mode in a guide
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between mode index and cutoff wavelength
questions.stem: Explain how the cutoff wavelength changes as the mode index increases

answer.exemplar: Cutoff wavelength is 2a over m, so as mode index m increases the cutoff wavelength decreases; each higher mode requires a shorter wavelength to fit across the guide.

questions.explanation: Higher modes have more half-wavelength variations across the width, requiring shorter wavelengths and thus higher frequencies.

questions.topic: What a guide does below its cutoff
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of below-cutoff attenuation and identify the trend

stimulus.body: Attenuation table: f/f_c = 0.5 attenuation 50 dB/m; 0.8 attenuation 15 dB/m; 0.9 attenuation 6 dB/m. License original.

questions.stem: What does the table imply as frequency approaches cutoff from below
questions.explanation: As frequency approaches cutoff from below, the evanescent decay weakens and attenuation drops. At cutoff attenuation is zero and propagation begins.

questions.topic: Mode and guide wavelength in a fed guide
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about guide wavelength and frequency
questions.stem: Stage one: what happens to guide wavelength as operating frequency rises far above cutoff; stage two: what is the limit

options.text: It shrinks; limit is free-space wavelength

questions.explanation: As frequency rises far above cutoff, the factor sqrt(1-(f_c/f)^2) approaches one, so guide wavelength approaches free-space wavelength from above.

questions.topic: Why the lowest mode is called dominant
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about why higher modes are avoided
questions.stem: Designers avoid higher modes in a waveguide because

options.text: They cause intermodal interference and dispersion

options.misconception: false; they carry power above cutoff

questions.explanation: Higher modes introduce multiple propagation paths with different phase velocities, causing dispersion and interference. Single-mode operation avoids this.

questions.topic: When conduction and displacement currents are comparable
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a material classification
questions.stem: A table classifies a material with ratio 0.5 as a good conductor; find the error

options.text: A ratio near one means comparable, not a good conductor

questions.explanation: A ratio of 0.5 is of order one, so conduction and displacement currents are comparable. A good conductor requires a ratio much greater than one.

questions.topic: Resistance of a wire at radio frequency
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute skin depth from a given resistance increase
questions.stem: A wire of radius 1 mm has AC resistance 10 times its DC resistance; estimate the skin depth in mm
questions.explanation: R_ac/R_dc equals r over (2 delta), so 10 equals 1 over (2 delta in mm), giving delta equals 0.05 mm. Using r over delta gives 0.1 mm.
questions.hint: delta equals r over 2 times ratio

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain cutoff in terms of transverse resonance
questions.stem: Explain cutoff frequency in terms of transverse resonance in a waveguide

answer.exemplar: Cutoff occurs when the transverse wavelength equals twice the guide width, so the wave fits exactly across; below this the transverse wavenumber is imaginary and propagation stops.

questions.explanation: The transverse standing-wave condition sets the minimum frequency. Below it the field cannot satisfy the boundary conditions with a real propagation constant.

questions.topic: Cutoff frequency of a rectangular guide
questions.learningObjective: Explain why TE10 is the dominant mode in terms of cutoff
questions.stem: Explain why TE10 is the dominant mode in a rectangular waveguide

answer.exemplar: TE10 has the lowest cutoff frequency because it has the longest cutoff wavelength, 2a, so it is the first mode to propagate as frequency rises from zero.

questions.explanation: The dominant mode is the one with lowest cutoff. TE10's half-wave variation across the width gives the longest allowable wavelength.
